issues.legal_issue: Conditional restrictions on transferring encumbered property do not preclude specific performance when the restriction can be satisfied and the seller has not proved an existing charge or amount due.
material_facts: The sellers argued that the land was subject to a cooperative society’s charge and could not be transferred.
They had not raised a specific issue or produced evidence establishing the alleged mortgage, the amount due, or the extent of any charge.
The applicable transfer restriction was conditional, and government permission for transfer could be granted.
The buyer could, under the applicable law, require redemption of a qualifying encumbrance and a valid discharge.
issues.conclusion: The alleged society charge and statutory transfer restrictions did not bar specific performance; the transfer could proceed subject to the required permissions and conditions.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48(d) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 restricts alienation until the society’s loan is repaid, but the restriction is conditional and does not prevent transfer once the loan is cleared. Sections 12(1)(c) and 12(2) of the Maharashtra Re-settlement of Project Displaced Persons Act, 1976 allow the Government to grant permission for transfer subject to conditions. Section 13(1)(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits a purchaser, in the specified circumstances, to compel the seller to redeem an encumbrance and obtain a valid discharge. The Court also relied on Nathulal v. Phoolchand, AIR 1970 SC 546, and drew an adverse inference from the sellers’ failure to produce evidence of the alleged charge.

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding concerns a buyer’s claim to compel completion of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.seller_produced_no_evidence_of_current_c: The seller alleged that the property was charged but produced no evidence establishing the current debt or the extent of the charge.
predicates.transfer_restriction_can_be_satisfied_by: The applicable restriction allows the transfer to proceed if required permission is obtained or a qualifying encumbrance is redeemed.

issues.definition: When a buyer seeks completion of a property sale, the seller does not prove a current charge, and the transfer restriction can be satisfied by permission or redemption, the restriction does not bar specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of fact supported by proper appreciation of the evidence are not reopened in an appeal under Article 136 absent legal infirmity.
material_facts: The trial court, first appellate court, and High Court made concurrent findings supporting the buyer’s account of the agreement and the parties’ performance.
The Supreme Court found those factual findings to be based on proper appreciation of the evidence and identified no legal infirmity in them.
The matter reached the Supreme Court by an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to revisit the concurrent factual findings.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court did not consider it appropriate to reopen questions of fact alone where the concurrent findings were based on proper appreciation of the evidence and disclosed no legal infirmity.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court under its discretionary appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings_are_evidence_ba: The courts below reached the same factual conclusions after considering the evidence.
predicates.no_legal_infirmity_is_shown: The appellant identifies no legal defect undermining those factual conclusions.

issues.definition: In an appeal under discretionary appellate jurisdiction, evidence-based concurrent factual findings without a shown legal defect are left undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A party’s unsupported assertion that signatures were obtained on blank papers as security for a loan does not displace findings supporting an agreement to sell, and a party seeking to challenge trial findings in a first appeal must use the proper appellate procedure.
material_facts: The sellers claimed that the buyer had obtained signatures on blank papers as security for a small loan rather than under an agreement to sell.
The sellers produced no cogent oral or documentary evidence to support that claim.
The trial court rejected the claim and found that the agreement to sell had been proved.
The sellers did not file cross-objections or an appeal challenging the trial court’s findings when the buyer appealed.
issues.conclusion: The unsupported blank-paper defence was rejected, and the sellers could not use the first appeal to challenge the trial court’s findings without cross-objections.
issues.legal_principle: The party asserting that signatures were obtained on blank papers as security bears the burden of proving that assertion. A party may support a decree before the first appellate court, but may not challenge adverse findings without filing cross-objections or an appeal.

predicates.property_sale_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over whether the parties made an agreement to sell property.
predicates.seller_asserted_signatures_were_obtained: The seller claimed that the other party obtained signatures on blank papers for a purpose other than the alleged sale agreement.
predicates.seller_produced_no_cogent_supporting_evi: The seller presented no persuasive oral or documentary evidence supporting that claim.
predicates.seller_filed_no_cross_objection_or_appea: The seller did not use a cross-objection or appeal to challenge adverse trial findings in the first appeal.

issues.definition: In a property sale dispute, an unsupported claim that signatures were obtained on blank papers is rejected, particularly when the seller also failed to challenge the adverse findings through the proper appellate procedure.

issues.legal_issue: An increase in property value does not by itself justify refusing specific performance when the buyer has proved readiness and willingness and the circumstances support equitable enforcement.
material_facts: The buyer proved the agreement, payment of earnest money, and readiness and willingness to perform her obligations.
The sellers failed to establish their defence that the agreement was fabricated from blank papers.
The sellers had retained the earnest money and enjoyed the property during the proceedings.
The buyer offered to pay substantially more than the original agreed consideration, and the Court found that offer fair and that it balanced the equities.
The sellers relied on the increase in the land’s market value as a reason to refuse specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld specific performance and directed completion on the basis of the buyer’s increased consideration offer, subject to the conditions imposed by the first appellate court.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 16(c) and 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 require proof of readiness and willingness and confer a discretion that must be exercised on settled equitable principles. Specific performance is not automatic merely because it is lawful; the Court considers the circumstances, conduct, and interests of the parties, and may refuse relief that gives an unfair advantage or causes unforeseen hardship. The Court relied on Bal Krishna v. Bhagwan Das, (2008) 12 SCC 145; Mohammadia Cooperative Building Society Ltd. v. Lakshmi Srinivasa Cooperative Building Society Ltd., (2008) 7 SCC 310; and P.V. Joseph’s son Mathew v. N. Kuruvila’s Son, AIR 1987 SC 2328. The Court held that an increase in market value alone did not justify refusal in the circumstances, particularly given the buyer’s increased offer.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and buyer_proved_readiness_and_willingness and seller_failed_to_prove_fabrication_defence and seller_retained_benefits_during_proceedings and buyer_offered_higher_consideration

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding concerns a buyer’s request to compel completion of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.buyer_proved_readiness_and_willingness: The buyer established that she was ready and willing to perform her contractual obligations.
predicates.seller_failed_to_prove_fabrication_defen: The seller did not prove the claim that the alleged sale agreement was fabricated from signatures obtained on blank papers.
predicates.seller_retained_benefits_during_proceedi: The seller kept the buyer’s earnest money and continued to enjoy the property while the proceedings were pending.
predicates.buyer_offered_higher_consideration: The buyer offered to pay more than the consideration stated in the agreement, and the Court regarded the offer as fair.

issues.definition: When a buyer proves readiness and willingness, the seller fails to prove a fabrication defence, the seller retains benefits during the proceedings, and the buyer offers higher consideration, specific performance may be granted on equitable terms despite increased property value.
